items.text: Our model achieves a new state-ofthe-art on an existing ACL anthology dataset (ACL-ARC) with a 13.3% absolute increase in F1 score, without relying on external linguistic resources or hand-engineered features as done in existing methods.
items.why: Claims a 13.3% absolute F1 gain without using hand-engineered features.
items.plain: Our model achieves a new best result on the ACL-ARC benchmark, increasing the F1 score by 13.3% absolute without relying on hand-crafted features or external linguistic resources.

items.text: Note that this scaffold task is different than simply adding section title as an additional feature in the input.
items.why: Distinguishes the section-title task from using section titles directly as features.
items.plain: This task differs from simply adding section titles as input features to the model.

items.text: 5We also experimented with adding section titles as additional feature to the input, however, it did not result in any improvements.
items.why: Reports an ablation finding that adding section titles as input features failed.
items.plain: We also tried adding section titles directly as input features, but it did not improve performance.

items.text: We later removed instances annotated with the OTHER option from our dataset (less than 1% of the annotated data), many of which were due to citation contexts which are incomplete or too short for the annotator to infer the citation intent.
items.why: Identifies dataset filtering criteria and potential data loss during annotation.
items.plain: We removed data marked as OTHER, which was less than 1% of the annotations and mainly consisted of incomplete or very short contexts.

items.text: To only collect high quality annotations, instances with conﬁdence score of ≤0.7 were discarded.
items.why: Notes that annotator instances with lower confidence scores were excluded.
items.plain: We removed any annotation instances that scored equal to or lower than 0.7 in confidence.

items.text: In addition, a subset of the dataset with 100 samples was re-annotated by a trained, expert annotator to check for quality, and the agreement rate with crowdsource workers was 86%.
items.why: States crowd-to-expert agreement rate on a small dataset sample.
items.plain: An expert re-annotated 100 samples, achieving an 86% agreement rate with the crowdsourced labels.

items.text: such as numbered citations (e.g., [1]) or name-year combinations (e.g, Lee et al (2012)) to not make the second task artiﬁcially easy by only detecting citation markers.
items.why: Explains a preprocessing step taken to avoid trivial shortcut features.
items.plain: We removed explicit citation markers like numbers or names and years so the model could not shortcut the task.

items.text: Section titles which did not map to any of the aforementioned titles were excluded from the dataset.
items.why: Reveals that unmapped section titles were dropped from the training data.
items.plain: Section titles that did not fit into our defined standard categories were excluded from the dataset.

items.text: To make sure our results are competitive with state-of-the-art results on this task, we also compare our model to Jurgens et al. (2018) which has the best reported results on the ACL-ARC dataset.
items.why: Identifies the primary previous state-of-the-art baseline model.
items.plain: We compare our method against Jurgens et al. (2018), which holds the best previously published results on the ACL-ARC dataset.

items.text: Our implementation of this model achieves a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.526 using 10-fold cross-validation, which is in line with the highest reported results in Jurgens et al. (2018): 0.53 using leave-oneout cross validation.
items.why: Explains a discrepancy between their baseline implementation and published cross-validation setups.
items.plain: Our implementation of Jurgens et al. (2018) achieved a 0.526 F1 score using 10-fold cross-validation, close to their reported 0.53 score using leave-one-out cross-validation.

items.text: leave-one-out cross validation in our experiments since it is impractical to re-train each variant of our deep learning models thousands of times.
items.why: Justifies changing evaluation protocol due to computational costs.
items.plain: We used a standard train, validation, and test split instead of leave-one-out cross-validation because re-training our deep learning models thousands of times was impractical.

items.text: We note that the scaffold tasks provide major contributions on top of the ELMo-enabled baseline (∆=13.6), demonstrating the efﬁcacy of using structural scaffolds for citation intent prediction.
items.why: Claims significant performance contributions specifically coming from scaffold tasks.
items.plain: Adding the scaffold tasks provided a 13.6 percentage point gain over the baseline that already included ELMo embeddings.

items.text: We also experimented with adding features used in Jurgens et al. (2018) to our best model and not only we did not see any improvements, but we observed
items.why: Reports that combining hand-engineered features with their best model yielded no gains.
items.plain: Adding the hand-engineered features from Jurgens et al. (2018) to our best model did not improve performance.

items.text: Note that this dataset is more than ﬁve times larger in size than the ACL-ARC, therefore the performance numbers are generally higher and the F1 gains are generally smaller since it is easier for the models to learn optimal parameters utilizing the larger annotated data.
items.why: Explains why gains on SciCite were smaller than on ACL-ARC.
items.plain: Because SciCite is much larger, overall scores are higher and F1 improvements are smaller because models learn effectively from the larger labeled set.

items.text: Generally we observe that results on categories with more number of instances are higher.
items.why: Notes a performance bias toward higher-frequency intent categories.
items.plain: Performance is generally higher on citation categories that have more training examples.

items.text: One general error pattern is that the model has more tendency to make false positive errors in the BACKGROUND category likely due to this category dominating both datasets.
items.why: Identifies a systematic error pattern caused by class imbalance.
items.plain: The model frequently produces false positives for the BACKGROUND class because it is the most frequent category in both datasets.

items.text: We experimented with encoding the extended surrounding context using a BiLSTM and concatenating it with the main citation context vector (z), but it resulted in a large decline in overall performance likely due to the overall noise introduced by the additional context.
items.why: Describes a failed attempt to incorporate surrounding context into the model.
items.plain: Concatenating encoded surrounding context into the main citation vector led to a large performance drop, likely due to added noise.
